title: Deep Discriminative Structure Proxy Hashing for Cross-modal Retrieval
claim: Traditional proxies are optimized in isolation against samples; structuring proxies into interacting relational groups sharpens each sample's discriminative response.
layout: 2 stacked panels, top-to-bottom, faded background with highlighted proxy cluster in ellipse
description: Two stacked dashed-border panels with rotated row labels on the left. The top panel, "Traditional Proxies", shows colored pill-shaped embedding vectors (blue, purple, pink, orange) scattered around black four-point star proxies. Each embedding connects to individual proxies by solid red lines (positive) and dashed teal lines (negative), with no links between proxies. The bottom panel, "Structured Proxies", repeats the layout but fades most embeddings, stars and edges to gray. A dashed ellipse picks out a cluster of four black proxies joined by black and purple edges, showing proxy-to-proxy interaction. One pink embedding at the lower right connects to that cluster by red, purple and teal edges. The eye goes first to the top panel's tangle of lines, then to the highlighted ellipse below.
caption: Motivation of the proposed structure-discriminative
abstract: Existing proxy-based hashing methods optimize samples toward independently learned proxies using isolated similarity constraints. Although efficient, this design overlooks the fact that proxies are learned jointly but lack explicit relational or competitive interactions during optimization. Consequently, proxy responses to a sample are often accumulated rather than contrasted, leading to weakly defined decision regions and limited discriminative structure in the Hamming space. In contrast, our method organizes multiple proxies into sample-specific relational structures, enabling proxies to interact and compete when responding to each sample. Through structure-guided learning, these interactions explicitly contrast positive and negative proxy responses, thereby shaping clearer and more discriminative decision boundaries. Extensive experiments on standard cross-modal benchmarks demonstrate that this structured discrimination consistently improves retrieval accuracy and embedding separability.
